c.tagline: Pink-stone capital in the shadow of Mount Ararat.

taxi.fareNote: App-based taxis (Yandex Go, GG) give fair metered fares; street/unmarked taxis may not use a meter - agree on the price before riding.

emergency.note: Fire: 101. Numbers work nationwide; English-speaking operator availability is limited outside tourist areas.

hood_landmark.Cascade / Opera District: Cafesjian Center for the Arts (Cascade Complex), Yerevan

avoid.reason: Use ride-hailing apps to dodge taxi overcharging and be aware of occasional political demonstrations around Republic Square.

hood_desc: The bustling downtown core packed with Republic Square, the Opera House, museums, restaurants and nightlife - best for first-time visitors who want everything walkable.
A hillside maze of centuries-old stone houses and cobbled lanes overlooking the Hrazdan gorge, right by the center - ideal for travelers wanting an atmospheric, off-beat old-town stay.
The area around the giant limestone Cascade stairway and its sculpture gardens, just north of downtown - quieter than Kentron but still an easy walk to attractions, great for art lovers.
A leafy hillside district around the Armenian Genocide memorial park, a short bus or taxi ride from downtown - suits visitors wanting green space and a slower, residential pace.
A budget-friendly outskirts district near the ancient Erebuni Fortress - best for travelers prioritizing low prices over a central location.
lodging: The Alexander, Luxury Collection Hotel, Yerevan

water.note: Sourced from mountain springs and well treated; tap water is generally safe and pleasant to drink.

transit.pay: Metro rides use tokens (jetons) bought at station counters. Bus and marshrutka fares are usually paid in cash directly to the driver. A unified electronic tap-card ticketing system has been rolling out across buses and the metro since 2025.
transit.hours: Metro and most buses run roughly 6:30am-11pm daily; there is no late-night rail service, so taxis and ride-hailing apps (Yandex Go, GG) cover the overnight gap.
transit.note: The compact 10-station Metro mainly serves outer districts and commuters; most visitors get around the walkable center on foot or by app-based taxi.

train: South Caucasus Railway - Yerevan Central Railway Station, with service to Gyumri and Tbilisi, Georgia
bus: Intercity marshrutka/coach buses from Kilikia Avtokayan Bus Station

tip.r: Not obligatory but 5-10% is appreciated at restaurants for good service; rounding up is common for taxis.

food.name: Khorovats
food.desc: Armenia's national barbecue: pork, lamb or veal skewered over vine-wood embers, plus whole aubergine and pepper grilled alongside and peeled hot.

places.name: Tavern Yerevan
places.note: Traditional dishes and live music; the first stop most visitors are sent to for khorovats.

places.name: Old Erivan
places.note: Period dining rooms and consistently excellent grilled meat.

places.name: Sherep
places.note: Chef Hamlet Petrosyan plates khorovats with wild herbs and pomegranate; book ahead.

food.name: Lavash
food.desc: Paper-thin bread slapped onto the wall of a clay tonir and peeled off in seconds. UNESCO-listed and used as plate, wrapper and utensil.

places.name: Lavash Restaurant
places.note: Tonir-baked fresh through service; the gold standard for traditional cooking at mid-range prices.

places.name: GUM Market
places.note: Covered food market where bakers sell stacks of lavash beside the dried fruit stalls.

places.name: Dolmama
places.note: Open since 1998 and dedicated to reviving traditional Armenian cooking.

food.name: Ghapama
food.desc: A whole pumpkin hollowed out, packed with rice, dried fruit, nuts and honey, baked until soft and cut open at the table. Autumn and feast food.

places.name: Tavern Yerevan
places.note: Keeps ghapama on the menu year-round alongside khorovats and pilaf.

places.name: Sherep
places.note: Modern reading of the dish from a kitchen built around Armenian tradition.

places.name: Tsirani Garden Restaurant
places.note: Garden setting with live traditional music, best in warm months.

food.name: Harissa
food.desc: Wheat and chicken beaten together over low heat for hours until it turns glossy and stretchy. A dish of remembrance, poured with melted butter.

places.name: Lavash Restaurant
places.note: Full traditional repertoire cooked with daily-sourced herbs and local meat.

places.name: Old Erivan
places.note: Traditional menu that keeps the older, slower dishes on.

places.name: Dolmama
places.note: Refined take on the classics in a townhouse dining room.

food.name: Tolma
food.desc: Vine or cabbage leaves rolled around spiced meat and rice; the summer pasuts version uses beans and lentils. Eaten with garlic yoghurt.

places.name: Dolmama
places.note: Named for the dish; the house tolma is its signature.

places.name: Lavash Restaurant
places.note: Serves the whole dolma family including the vegetarian pasuts version.

places.name: Tavern Yerevan
places.note: Large portions and a lively room; reliable version of the classic.

food.name: Gata and dried fruit
food.desc: Sweet layered gata pastry alongside Armenia's famous sujukh, dried apricots and walnut preserves - the standard end to any meal.

places.name: GUM Market
places.note: Rows of vendors offering endless free samples of sujukh, fruit leather and dried apricot.

places.name: Ponchik Monchik
places.note: Popular local chain for cream-filled doughnuts and sweet pastries.

places.name: Vernissage market stalls
places.note: Weekend market with home bakers selling gata beside the crafts.

food.name: Armenian brandy
food.desc: Grape brandy aged in Caucasian oak, made in Yerevan since 1887 and the country's most famous export. Drunk neat, after dinner.

places.name: Yerevan Brandy Company
places.note: The historic hilltop factory runs guided cellar tours ending in a tasting.

places.name: In Vino
places.note: Armenia's first wine bar and merchant, with a deep spirits shelf too.

places.name: Wine Republic
places.note: Hub for tastings and seminars on Armenian drinks history.

food.name: Areni wine
food.desc: Red made from the native Areni Noir grape, grown near the world's oldest known winery. Light-bodied, high acid, increasingly good.

places.name: In Vino
places.note: Over 1,000 labels and daily-changing flights of six Armenian wines with cheese.

places.name: Wine Republic
places.note: Broad Armenian list poured by the glass alongside an eclectic kitchen.

places.name: Saryan Street wine bars
places.note: The whole street is bars and tasting rooms; tables spill outside all summer.

landmarks: Republic Square
Yerevan's grand central plaza, ringed by pink and cream tufa-stone buildings, comes alive each evening with a choreographed singing fountain show.
Cascade Complex
This giant tiered limestone stairway doubles as an outdoor art museum and viewpoint, rewarding the climb with sculptures and sweeping city views toward Mount Ararat.
Tsitsernakaberd (Armenian Genocide Memorial)
This somber hilltop memorial with its twelve leaning basalt slabs and eternal flame is Armenia's most solemn and emotionally powerful pilgrimage site.
Matenadaran
This repository of ancient Armenian manuscripts houses priceless illuminated texts dating back centuries, standing as a monument to the nation's literary heritage.
Yerevan Opera Theatre
This elegant circular building anchors the city's cultural district, its surrounding square and lake making it a favorite gathering spot at any hour.
Blue Mosque
The only surviving Persian-style mosque in Yerevan, its turquoise-tiled dome and tranquil courtyard garden offer a peaceful escape from the busy streets.
Vernissage Market
This sprawling open-air weekend bazaar overflows with handwoven carpets, Soviet antiques, and folk art, offering a vivid slice of Armenian craft and culture.
Saint Gregory the Illuminator Cathedral
One of the largest Armenian Apostolic churches in the world, this modern cathedral impresses with its soaring stone architecture and ornate interior frescoes.
Erebuni Fortress
Founded in 782 BC, these ancient Urartian ruins predate the Armenian capital itself and offer sweeping views along with a glimpse into the region's deep history.
Swan Lake
This artificial lake in the city center, home to graceful swans, transforms into an ice rink in winter and is ringed by cafes perfect for people-watching.

intl.to: Tbilisi (Georgia), extended to Batumi in summer

train.note: Trains leave from Yerevan (Sasuntsi Davit) station. The only international line runs north to Georgia: an overnight sleeper to Tbilisi (roughly every other day), extended to the Black Sea coast at Batumi as a seasonal summer service (about mid-June to early October). The borders with Turkey and Azerbaijan are closed, so no trains run west or east.

bus.note: Most international buses and marshrutka minibuses use Kilikia Central Bus Station. Envoy runs a comfortable daily shuttle to Tbilisi (~6h); shared minibuses also run to Tbilisi and long-distance buses head to Tehran (Iran). Carry your passport for the Georgian or Iranian border - there is no online booking for the informal minibus services.

ferry.note: Armenia is landlocked, so there are no international ferries. Lake Sevan has only local pleasure boats in summer.

half.name: Geghard Monastery
half.blurb: A UNESCO-listed medieval monastery partly carved from the cliffs of the dramatic Azat Valley.

half.name: Garni Temple
half.blurb: A first-century Greco-Roman temple perched above a gorge lined with striking basalt columns.

half.name: Khor Virap
half.blurb: A hilltop monastery offering Armenia's most iconic close-up views of snowcapped Mount Ararat.

half.name: Lake Sevan
half.blurb: The Caucasus's largest lake, a high-altitude expanse with sandy beaches and a peninsula monastery.

half.name: Etchmiadzin
half.blurb: The spiritual capital of Armenia, home to an ancient cathedral central to the Apostolic Church.

half.name: Noravank
half.blurb: A thirteenth-century monastery set dramatically against towering brick-red cliffs in a narrow gorge.
